case.title: Elizabeth line / Crossrail — M4A Internal Evidence Case
case.scope_question: What do inspectable public records support about the Elizabeth line's transport-capacity and realised-use benefits, its public-resource burden, and the delivery tradeoffs created by cost growth and delay?
limitations: This M4A case is deliberately narrow and does not attempt a full ex-post economic appraisal of the Elizabeth line.

Usage and capacity evidence demonstrates substantial realised transport use, but it does not by itself establish the full distribution of economic benefits across households, businesses, regions, or income groups.
The cost and schedule record is drawn mainly from the UK National Audit Office and official sponsor publications; this case does not allocate moral blame to people or contractors.
The case does not yet incorporate a complete lifecycle carbon account, property-value distribution analysis, accessibility-by-income analysis, or full counterfactual transport model.
No Cooperation Index, project score, person score, motive finding, or moral identity label is supported by this record.

subjects.public_role_context: A major London rail infrastructure programme, now operating as the Elizabeth line, used here as a project-level Behavior Atlas case. The subject is the project footprint, not any person's moral identity.
notes: The case focuses on realised transport use and capacity alongside public-resource, cost-growth, and schedule evidence.
No person is a Behavior Atlas subject in this bundle.

claims.statement: At the 2022 opening, the UK Department for Transport said the Elizabeth line would increase central London rail capacity by 10% and substantially reduce some cross-London journey times.
The Department for Transport described the Elizabeth line project cost at opening as almost £19 billion, with £9 billion of government investment.
Transport for London reported 242 million Elizabeth line journeys in 2025/26 and more than 800 million journeys since opening.
In 2019, the National Audit Office concluded that Crossrail's delivery approach had driven unnecessary costs and damaged public value, while recording a substantial increase in the funding package.

The National Audit Office reported in 2021 that the central section was expected to open up to three and a half years later than originally planned and that the funding package had reached £18.8 billion.

assessments.rationale: The record supports substantial transport-capacity and realised-use benefits, while also showing a very large project cost and public financing burden. The current evidence does not compare benefits and burdens across households, income groups, businesses, or regions on a like-for-like basis, so the distributional direction remains mixed.

The operating railway is heavily used and has added major rail capacity, demonstrating that the investment produced a functioning high-demand public asset. Counterevidence is material: the NAO documented cost growth, schedule slippage, and delivery choices that damaged public value. The present case therefore identifies a real stewardship tradeoff rather than a single positive or negative verdict.

review_events.reason: Create a second real project-level case for M4A plurality testing from official UK sponsor, audit, and operator records, with no public-alpha release.
Confirm that each claim resolves to inspectable source evidence, that benefit and burden evidence remain visible together, and that no person-level judgment or composite score is introduced.
